People who are not pregnant (WHO/IDF criteria) — WHO: 6.1–6.9 mmol/L; 2-hour glucose, if measured, < 7.8 mmol/L. The ADA/NIDDK lower limit is 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L).

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Prediabetes and diabetes are the most common causes. Other possible causes include an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism), pancreatic problems including pancreatitis, stress from surgery, very serious illness or trauma, adrenal gland problems and certain medicines.
With diabetes: some diabetes medicines and other glucose-lowering medicines, not eating enough (especially after taking diabetes medicine) and more physical activity than usual.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Without diabetes, low glucose is uncommon; possible causes include liver or kidney disease, underactive adrenal glands, some pituitary disorders, an underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism), malnutrition, certain medicines and alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
bullets: Limitations: What a result means depends on which test was done, other test results and the medical history.

slides.title: Functions of carbohydrates
bullets: Energy source: the energy needed by the brain, blood cells, kidneys and adrenal glands comes from the oxidation of glucose; complete breakdown of 1 g of carbohydrate releases about 17 kJ (4.1 kcal).
Structural role: carbohydrates form part of cell membranes and intracellular structures and take part in the synthesis of nucleoproteins, lipids and enzymes.
Storage: starch in plants, glycogen in animals and humans; the liver and muscles are the main glycogen stores.

slides.title: Functions of carbohydrates
bullets: Protective role: mucus secreted by glands (mucopolysaccharides) protects the walls of the stomach, intestine, oesophagus and bronchi from mechanical damage.
Regulatory role: fibre mechanically stimulates the gastric and intestinal mucosa and increases motility.
Specific roles: nerve-impulse conduction, antibody formation, blood-group specificity.

slides.title: Classification of carbohydrates
bullets: Monosaccharides are single sugar molecules; by carbon number they are trioses, tetroses, pentoses and hexoses. Hexoses include glucose, fructose and galactose.

Glucose is the main carbohydrate and a building block of many others (lactose, sucrose, starch and more). Galactose is a spatial isomer of glucose (it differs at the fourth carbon atom) and is converted to glucose more easily in the liver. Fructose is fruit sugar.
Oligosaccharides (disaccharides): sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose; maltose = two glucose units.

slides.title: Classification of carbohydrates
bullets: Polysaccharides: homopolysaccharides consist of one kind of monosaccharide — starch and glycogen (from glucose), fibre (cellulose); heteropolysaccharides include the mucopolysaccharides, for example heparin.

Glycogen is the main storage carbohydrate of humans and animals; its structure resembles amylopectin but is more branched; it accumulates in the liver, muscle and heart and is broken down quickly when glucose is lacking.

slides.title: Digestion and absorption of carbohydrates
bullets: Digestion starts in the mouth under salivary amylase and maltase, but because food stays in the mouth only briefly this stage is limited.
Carbohydrates are not digested in the stomach — it has no enzymes that catalyse this process.
Most digestion takes place in the small intestine: pancreatic and intestinal juice enzymes and a weakly alkaline medium are favourable for carbohydrate hydrolysis.
Fibre is not broken down in the small intestine: it passes to the colon, helps form stool and is excreted.

slides.title: Digestion and absorption of carbohydrates
bullets: Glucose passes from the liver into the blood and is delivered to organs and tissues. The kidney reabsorbs glucose almost completely, so normally it is not lost in the urine.

slides.title: Blood glucose and its regulation
bullets: Most of the monosaccharides in blood are glucose; carbohydrate transformations in tissues start from glucose, so it is the most important indicator of carbohydrate metabolism.
Blood glucose is notably stable: any change in carbohydrate metabolism shows up as a change in its blood level.
The central nervous system (responding to external and internal stimuli) and hormones take part in regulation.
Insulin raises the permeability of cell membranes to glucose, increases its use by cells and lowers its level in the blood.

slides.title: Blood glucose and its regulation
bullets: The liver has a special role: when glucose is lacking, glycogen is broken down and the blood is enriched with glucose; when glucose is in excess, the liver converts it to glycogen.

slides.title: Disorders of carbohydrate metabolism
bullets: Hyperglycaemia — raised blood glucose: from excessive carbohydrate intake or poor use by cells. It can be physiological (large carbohydrate intake, short-lived) or pathological (diabetes mellitus, mental illness, brain tumour and others).
Glucosuria — glucose appearing in the urine: when the blood level exceeds the renal threshold, the kidney tubules cannot reabsorb the excess.
Hypoglycaemia — lowered blood glucose: excess insulin (given from outside or overproduced), some hypothalamic tumours, liver damage, heavy physical work. A sharp fall leads to coma.

slides.title: Disorders of carbohydrate metabolism
bullets: Diabetes mellitus: the main cause is disturbed regulation of insulin metabolism; glucose cannot enter cells and builds up in the blood (hyperglycaemia, glucosuria) while cells starve for energy.

Compensation: gluconeogenesis increases, acetyl-CoA accumulates and ketone (acetone) bodies form — ketonaemia and ketonuria; blood pH shifts to the acid side (acidosis), the breath smells of acetone, and in severe cases diabetic coma develops.

slides.title: Laboratory assessment of carbohydrate metabolism
bullets: The main test is blood glucose. The book distinguishes methods: the Hagedorn–Jensen method is non-specific (it measures all reducing substances); the ortho-toluidine and glucose-oxidase methods measure true glucose.

Glucose loading test: blood is taken fasting, a glucose load is given and the sugar is measured again at set intervals to draw a sugar curve. In a healthy person a moderate rise returns to normal; in diabetes the fasting level is high and after the load stays high for a long time. The load and timings in the book may differ from current recommendations — see the OGTT card in the app for the current procedure.

slides.title: Laboratory assessment of carbohydrate metabolism
bullets: Lactic acid reflects tissue oxygen supply: it rises after prolonged physical exertion and in diseases with breathlessness. Pyruvate rises in thiamine (B1) deficiency (beriberi).
Ketone bodies occur in diabetes mellitus, fasting, pregnancy and toxaemias.
Glucose is normally absent from urine: its appearance points to hyperglycaemia or kidney damage.

slides.title: In which process is the main amount of glucose utilized:
Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
bullets: 1. Classification of carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose), oligosaccharides and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, fiber); complex carbohydrates – glycoproteins, glycosaminoglycans.

2. Biological significance: the main source of energy (glucose is the main substrate for the brain and erythrocytes), storage (glycogen), structural and receptor functions (glycoproteins, glycolipids).

slides.title: Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
bullets: 3. Digestion: in the mouth salivary α-amylase starts it, in the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down starch, brush-border enzymes (maltase, isomaltase, sucrase, lactase) hydrolyze to monosaccharides.

4. Absorption: glucose and galactose – with Na⁺ via SGLT1 (secondary active transport), fructose – passively via GLUT5; from the enterocyte into the blood through basolateral transporters, then via the portal vein to the liver.

slides.title: Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
bullets: 5. Clinical-laboratory link: in lactase deficiency and other disaccharidase deficiencies – osmotic diarrhea; starch in stool (amylorrhea) – a sign of digestive insufficiency; blood glucose is measured by modern enzymatic methods (hexokinase, glucose oxidase).

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Glucose homeostasis: insulin (β cells) is the only glucose-lowering hormone: it enhances glucose entry into tissues, glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; counter-regulatory hormones – glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroid hormones.
2. Nervous system: sympathetic activity (adrenaline) enhances glycogenolysis and glucagon secretion; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) increase insulin secretion after a meal.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 3. Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β cells, absolute insulin deficiency; markers: autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8), low C-peptide; tendency to ketoacidosis.
4. Type 2 DM – insulin resistance and relative insulin secretion deficiency; associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome; C-peptide initially normal/high.
5. Other types: gestational DM, monogenic (MODY), diseases of the exocrine pancreas, drug- or endocrinopathy-related.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 6. Diagnostic criteria are the same for both types: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT 2-hour value ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms.

slides.title: Methods of determining glucose?
bullets: 1. Enzymatic methods are the modern standard: the hexokinase method (glucose → glucose-6-phosphate → with G6PD, NAD(P)H is formed, 340 nm) – the most specific and accurate, widely used on automated analyzers.

2. Glucose oxidase–peroxidase (GOD-POD): glucose is oxidized to form H2O2, peroxidase with a chromogen gives a colored product; prone to interference from reducing substances such as ascorbate and urate; many glucometers are also GOD-based.
3. Samples: venous plasma (diagnostic standard), serum, capillary blood (glucometer – for monitoring); whole-blood and plasma results differ.

slides.title: Methods of determining glucose?
bullets: 4. Preanalytics: glycolysis (~5–7%/hour at room temperature) – separate the plasma within 30–60 minutes or use a tube with NaF (NaF needs time to take full effect).
5. Normal fasting venous plasma is about 3.9–5.6 mmol/L (70–100 mg/dL; depends on the laboratory); ADA: 5.6–6.9 – impaired fasting glucose, ≥7.0 – diabetes criterion; <3.9 – level 1 hypoglycemia.
6. Internal quality control: two-level control materials, Westgard rules; participation in external quality assessment.
